collection.title: Awareness, selfhood, metacognition, social cognition, comparative cognition, and machine-mind gap audit
collection.scope: Provisional records absent from the 2026-08-29 Noemorph base catalog. The collection prioritizes awareness, metacognition, selfhood, developmental and comparative social cognition, and machine theory-of-mind. One adjacent attention theory is retained with an explicit boundary note.
collection.method: Exact-name and keyword audit of the base catalog followed by source verification against DOI publisher records, official proceedings, and peer-reviewed primary or authoritative review literature.
collection.attribution_policy: Each record preserves its own proponents, claim scope, evidence profile, and citations. No inter-theory relationship, convergence, or synthesis claim is asserted.

records.name: Partial Awareness Hypothesis
records.status_note: The proposal remains a live account of graded and level-specific access, but evidence depends on how representational level, report, and subjective visibility are operationalized.
records.summary: Conscious access can occur independently at different levels of a representational hierarchy. An observer may therefore access some features of a stimulus while lacking access to higher-level identity or a fully integrated object representation, yielding partial rather than wholly present or absent awareness.
records.boundary_note: This is a hypothesis about the grain and level of conscious access. It is not the same claim as phenomenal overflow, and it does not by itself specify a neural mechanism or a metaphysics of consciousness.
records.claim_scope: Human visual awareness under masking and related psychophysical manipulations; specifically, whether access is graded across independently accessible representational levels.
records.evidence_profile: Psychophysical visibility reports, objective discrimination, masking, and manipulations of task-relevant processing level.
open_questions: Which experimental signatures uniquely distinguish partial awareness from response noise or mixed all-or-none states?
How stable is level-specific awareness across stimulus classes, report formats, and no-report measures?
Does partial access generalize beyond visual perception?

records.name: Nelson–Narens Monitoring–Control Framework
records.status_note: The two-level architecture remains foundational in metacognition research, while particular monitoring cues and control policies are modeled differently across tasks.
records.summary: Cognition is organized into an object level and a meta level. Information flowing from the object level to the meta level supports monitoring, while control signals from the meta level modify object-level operations such as study, retrieval, reporting, or termination.
records.boundary_note: The framework was developed for metacognition and metamemory. It does not entail that every monitoring signal is phenomenally conscious, nor is it a general theory of phenomenal consciousness.
records.claim_scope: Monitoring and strategic control of first-order cognitive operations, especially learning, memory retrieval, confidence, and voluntary reporting.
records.evidence_profile: Judgments of learning, feeling-of-knowing reports, confidence, optional reporting, study-time allocation, retrieval termination, and accuracy–quantity tradeoffs.
open_questions: Which monitoring signals are consciously accessible and which remain implicit?
How should reciprocal monitoring and control be implemented computationally across cognitive domains?
When do reports reflect monitoring quality rather than control policy or response incentives?

citations.title: Metamemory: A theoretical framework and new findings
Monitoring and control processes in the strategic regulation of memory accuracy

records.name: Meta-d′ and Metacognitive-Efficiency Framework
records.status: widely used measurement framework · assumptions actively debated
records.status_note: Meta-d′ and meta-d′/d′ are standard tools for separating confidence sensitivity from first-order performance, but estimates depend on signal-detection assumptions, trial counts, rating structure, and model specification.
records.summary: Meta-d′ expresses how much first-order signal, in d′ units, would be required for an ideal observer to produce the observed confidence discrimination between correct and incorrect decisions. Dividing meta-d′ by d′ yields an estimate of metacognitive efficiency relative to task sensitivity.
records.boundary_note: This is an inferential and measurement framework, not a substantive theory that confidence constitutes consciousness. High or low meta-d′ alone does not establish the presence or absence of phenomenal awareness.
records.claim_scope: Quantification of metacognitive sensitivity and efficiency from confidence or other type-2 judgments while controlling for first-order task sensitivity and response bias.
records.evidence_profile: Confidence-rating distributions, type-1 and type-2 receiver-operating characteristics, hierarchical model fits, and cross-task or cross-population comparisons.
open_questions: How robust are efficiency estimates when equal-variance and stationarity assumptions fail?
Which latent processes—evidence loss, additional noise, criterion variability, or post-decisional evidence—produce a given meta-d′ deficit?
How should meta-d′ be adapted for continuous, multi-alternative, or nonverbal reports?

citations.title: A signal detection theoretic approach for estimating metacognitive sensitivity from confidence ratings
How to measure metacognition
citations.authors: Stephen M. Fleming; Hakwan C. Lau

records.name: Bayesian Second-Order Self-Evaluation Framework
records.status_note: The framework provides a normative account of confidence and error monitoring, while the brain's approximations, evidence sources, and task-specific departures from optimality remain under investigation.
records.summary: Self-evaluation is modeled as Bayesian inference about the performance of a coupled but distinct first-order decision system. Confidence and error detection combine a separate evidence sample with information about one's own choice, allowing dissociations between decision accuracy and metacognitive judgment without treating confidence as a direct readout of the decision variable.
records.boundary_note: This decision self-evaluation framework is distinct from the cataloged Higher-Order State Space account: its target is confidence and error monitoring about decisions, not the higher-order inference proposed to generate awareness itself.
records.claim_scope: Human confidence, error detection, and metacognitive calibration in perceptual and value-based decisions.
records.evidence_profile: Bayesian ideal-observer modeling, confidence distributions, error reports, performance–confidence dissociations, and comparison of fitted latent evidence variables.
open_questions: What neural computations approximate the proposed second-order inference?
When does confidence use the same evidence as choice versus post-decisional or action-related evidence?
How does the framework generalize to memory, learning, and social self-evaluation?

citations.authors: Stephen M. Fleming; Nathaniel D. Daw

records.name: Self-Memory System
records.tradition: Autobiographical memory / cognitive psychology of self
records.status_note: The Self-Memory System continues to organize research on autobiographical remembering, identity, and goal regulation; its component structure and neural implementation are still refined.
records.summary: Autobiographical memories are transient constructions produced by interaction between an autobiographical knowledge base and a working self composed of current goals and self-images. The knowledge base constrains who one has been and can be, while the working self regulates access to memory in the service of coherence and adaptive correspondence.
records.boundary_note: The framework explains autobiographical memory and diachronic self-representation. It does not reduce all selfhood to narrative memory and does not claim that memory construction alone explains phenomenal consciousness.
records.claim_scope: Construction, retrieval, organization, and self-regulation of autobiographical memories and their contribution to temporally extended identity.
records.evidence_profile: Autobiographical recall, memory specificity, goal effects, clinical and neuropsychological dissociations, lifespan development, and neuroimaging of autobiographical remembering.
open_questions: How are working-self goals implemented and updated neurally?
How does the system balance accurate correspondence with self-coherence under conflict?
Which parts of autobiographical construction require autonoetic consciousness?

citations.title: The construction of autobiographical memories in the self-memory system
citations.authors: Martin A. Conway; Christopher W. Pleydell-Pearce

citations.title: Memory and the self

records.name: Neisser's Multiple-Selves Framework
records.status_note: The taxonomy remains influential in developmental and embodied-self research, though the proposed informational separability and direct-perception claims are not a settled consensus.
records.summary: Self-knowledge arises from multiple informational sources rather than a single self-representation. Neisser distinguishes ecological, interpersonal, extended, private, and conceptual selves; the ecological and interpersonal selves are proposed to emerge early through information specifying one's relation to the physical and social environment.
records.boundary_note: The ecological and interpersonal self are perceptual organizations of self-related information, not equivalent to explicit self-concept, narrative identity, mirror recognition, or reflective phenomenal self-consciousness.
records.claim_scope: Sources and developmental trajectories of self-knowledge, especially directly perceived bodily–environmental and interpersonal relations.
records.evidence_profile: Ecological perception, visual–proprioceptive contingency, infant social interaction, developmental observation, and conceptual analysis of distinct self-information sources.
open_questions: To what degree are ecological and interpersonal self-information directly specified rather than inferentially represented?
How do the five proposed selves interact across development?
Which components are necessary for explicit or phenomenal self-awareness?

citations.title: Five kinds of self-knowledge
Two perceptually given aspects of the self and their development

records.name: Joint Attention
records.status_note: Joint attention is a mature research domain, but definitions and measures distinguish gaze following, responding to joint attention, initiating joint attention, and sustained joint engagement.
records.summary: Joint attention is the coordination of two individuals' attention with respect to an object or event, including behavior that follows, directs, or sustains another's attention and, in stronger formulations, represents the focus as shared. It is a major developmental context for communication and social learning.
records.boundary_note: Gaze following alone need not demonstrate awareness that attention is mutually shared. Joint attention is related to, but not identical with, full belief attribution, shared intentionality, or phenomenal consciousness.
records.claim_scope: Development and function of coordinated attention in infant–caregiver interaction, communication, reference, learning, and later social cognition.
records.evidence_profile: Gaze and point following, alternating gaze, declarative and imperative gestures, joint engagement, longitudinal language outcomes, and developmental or clinical comparison.
open_questions: Which behavioral criteria distinguish shared-attention representation from directional cue following?
How do initiating and responding to joint attention rely on different mechanisms?
Which aspects are shared with nonhuman animals and which depend on human communicative norms?

records.name: False-Belief Understanding
records.status_note: Explicit false-belief tasks remain central operational measures, but performance is influenced by language, executive demand, task format, and population-specific factors; task failure is not a sufficient diagnosis of absent theory of mind.
records.summary: False-belief understanding is the capacity to represent that another agent's belief can differ from reality and from one's own knowledge, and to use that attributed belief when predicting or explaining the agent's action. Classic unexpected-transfer tasks operationalize explicit belief attribution.
records.boundary_note: This record catalogs a target construct and experimental family, not a unitary theory of mind. A correct response does not exhaust theory-of-mind competence, and an incorrect response does not by itself establish mindblindness or lack of social understanding.
records.claim_scope: Explicit tracking and action prediction based on another person's mistaken belief, principally in developmental and clinical experimental tasks.
records.evidence_profile: Unexpected-transfer and unexpected-contents tasks, verbal prediction and explanation, anticipatory behavior, developmental trajectories, task-manipulation studies, and clinical comparisons.
open_questions: How much performance variance reflects belief representation versus language and executive control?
Do implicit and explicit false-belief paradigms measure the same capacity?
How should tasks be adapted without treating neurodivergent social cognition as a global deficit?

records.name: Teleological Stance and Naïve Theory of Rational Action
records.status_note: Evidence supports early sensitivity to goal efficiency and situational constraints, while debate continues over whether those findings require teleological representation, mental-state attribution, lower-level perceptual mechanisms, or learned expectations.
records.summary: Young infants interpret actions by relating an observed movement, a goal state, and situational constraints through a principle of rational action: agents are expected to select an efficient available means to their goal. The early teleological stance is proposed as nonmentalistic and developmentally prior to a later stance that represents beliefs and desires.
records.boundary_note: The teleological stance explicitly analyzes action without initially attributing propositional mental states. It is therefore distinct from Dennett's intentional stance, full belief–desire mindreading, and the cataloged Theory-Theory family.
records.claim_scope: Infant and adult interpretation of goal-directed action under constraints, especially expectations of rational efficiency.
records.evidence_profile: Habituation and violation-of-expectation paradigms, goal-change and constraint manipulations, referential action studies, and developmental comparison.
open_questions: What evidence distinguishes principle-based teleological reasoning from perceptual novelty or learned action regularities?
When and how does nonmentalistic teleology develop into explicit belief–desire attribution?
How domain-specific is the rational-action principle?

citations.title: The teleological origins of mentalistic action explanations: A developmental hypothesis
Teleological reasoning in infancy: The naïve theory of rational action

records.name: Bayesian Theory of Mind and Inverse Planning
records.status_note: The framework quantitatively predicts judgments in controlled action-understanding tasks, while its approximate-rationality assumptions and generalization to natural social behavior remain active research issues.
records.summary: Observers are modeled as inverting a generative model in which an agent plans approximately rationally given its beliefs, desires, percepts, and environment. Bayesian inference combines observed actions with priors to recover probability distributions over those latent mental states.
records.boundary_note: This is a specific probabilistic formalization of mental-state inference. It is not merely an alias for Theory-Theory, Dennett's intentional stance, or the teleological stance, and model success does not establish that people explicitly compute the fitted Bayesian quantities.
records.claim_scope: Quantitative attribution of goals, beliefs, desires, and percepts from observed action under a generative model of approximately rational planning.
records.evidence_profile: Behavioral probability judgments, animated-maze and choice tasks, generative model comparison, inverse planning, and quantitative prediction of belief–desire attribution.
open_questions: How are priors and subjective models of other agents learned?
How does inference handle irrationality, habit, emotion, communication, and norm-following?
Which computational approximations can scale to continuous, multi-agent social environments?

records.name: Mindshaping Account of Social Cognition
records.tradition: Philosophy of cognitive science / cultural evolution
records.status_note: Mindshaping is a developed alternative emphasis within social-cognition theory, but the claimed explanatory priority of regulative practices over sophisticated mindreading remains contested.
records.summary: Human social cognition relies not only on reading already formed minds but on practices that shape dispositions, expectations, narratives, and norms so that behavior becomes easier to coordinate and interpret. On the stronger account, sophisticated propositional-attitude attribution depends developmentally and evolutionarily on prior mindshaping practices.
records.boundary_note: Mindshaping is not an alias for mindreading, interaction theory, social conformity, or collective intentionality. Its distinctive claim concerns the explanatory and evolutionary role of practices that make minds behaviorally interpretable.
records.claim_scope: Developmental, cultural, and evolutionary functions of imitation, pedagogy, norm enforcement, expectation, and narrative in stabilizing socially interpretable cognition and behavior.
records.evidence_profile: Philosophical argument drawing on developmental psychology, social psychology, cultural evolution, niche construction, pedagogy, imitation, norm conformity, and narrative self-constitution.
open_questions: How should mindshaping be operationalized independently of mindreading and ordinary social influence?
Which regulative practices are necessary for propositional-attitude attribution?
What comparative and developmental evidence would distinguish causal priority from reciprocal co-development?

citations.title: Mindreading, Mindshaping, and Evolution
Mindshaping: A New Framework for Understanding Human Social Cognition

records.name: Natural Pedagogy
records.status_note: Sensitivity to ostensive communication is well studied, while the strength of kind-generalization biases, cultural universality, human specificity, and status as an evolved adaptation remain debated.
records.summary: Human communication is proposed to include a specialized system for transmitting generic, cognitively opaque cultural knowledge. Infants are receptive to ostensive signals that mark communication, expect a referential target, and tend to interpret ostensive demonstrations as conveying kind-relevant and generalizable information.
records.boundary_note: Natural pedagogy is a theory of communicative social learning, not a general theory of consciousness. It is distinct from all teaching behavior, imitation alone, shared intentionality, and the broader claim that learning is social.
records.claim_scope: Infant and human receptivity to ostensive–referential communication and the transmission of generic cultural knowledge.
records.evidence_profile: Eye contact and infant-directed communication, gaze and reference, imitation of causally opaque actions, object-function learning, generalization tests, and cross-cultural or comparative studies.
open_questions: When do ostensive cues promote generic learning versus episodic or person-specific learning?
How culturally variable are the cues and resulting inductive biases?
Does evidence support a human-specific evolved adaptation rather than interacting general mechanisms?

citations.title: Natural pedagogy
Natural pedagogy as evolutionary adaptation

records.name: Mirror Self-Recognition and the Mark Test
records.status: widely used paradigm · construct interpretation contested
records.status_note: The mark test is a historically important operational assay of visual self-recognition. Species conclusions and inferences from task success or failure remain sensitive to sensory ecology, motivation, experience, and the definition of self-awareness.
records.summary: After experience with a mirror, an individual may use the reflected image to inspect or touch a covert mark that cannot otherwise be seen. Such mark-directed behavior is treated as evidence that the subject relates the image to its own body rather than treating it only as another individual.
records.boundary_note: Mirror self-recognition is an operational indicator of visual self-recognition, not a sufficient test of phenomenal consciousness, a unitary self-concept, or general self-awareness. Failure cannot rule out nonvisual forms of self-knowledge.
records.claim_scope: Visual recognition of one's reflected body in human development and comparative animal cognition.
records.evidence_profile: Mirror exposure, contingency testing, covert-mark behavior, developmental sequences, species comparison, modified sensory paradigms, and replication or critique of mark-directed responses.
open_questions: What cognitive representation is minimally required for mark-directed behavior?
How should the paradigm be adapted for species whose primary sensory ecology is not visual?
Which aspects of self-recognition generalize beyond mirrors and body appearance?

citations.title: Chimpanzees: Self-Recognition
Mirror self-image reactions before age two

records.name: Comparative Animal Metacognition and Uncertainty Monitoring
records.status: active and methodologically contested research program
records.status_note: Multiple species show adaptive uncertainty or information-seeking behavior, but whether particular results require metacognitive monitoring rather than associative, behavioral-cue, or response-competition accounts is evaluated paradigm by paradigm.
records.summary: Comparative metacognition research tests whether nonhuman animals monitor the strength or availability of their own perceptual and memory information. Subjects may decline difficult trials, seek information, or selectively take memory tests; transfer and cue-control procedures aim to distinguish internal monitoring from learned external associations.
records.boundary_note: Adaptive uncertainty responses do not automatically establish explicit metarepresentation, human-like self-reflection, or phenomenal consciousness. The record concerns a research framework and target capacity, not a single mechanism shared across species.
records.claim_scope: Behavioral monitoring of uncertainty, perceptual difficulty, memory availability, and information need in nonhuman animals.
records.evidence_profile: Uncertainty-response and opt-out tasks, prospective and retrospective wagering, information seeking, optional memory tests, transfer tests, cue controls, species comparison, and associative-model challenges.
open_questions: Which paradigms exclude public-cue and reinforcement-history explanations most convincingly?
Do uncertainty monitoring and metamemory share a domain-general process within individual animals?
What level of self-representation, if any, is required for successful performance?

records.name: ToMnet Machine Theory-of-Mind Architecture
records.status_note: ToMnet established a learnable agent-modeling architecture in controlled gridworlds. Later machine-ToM research broadens tasks and evaluation, but general, grounded, and robust mental-state modeling remains unresolved.
records.summary: A Theory-of-Mind network meta-learns to model agents from behavioral observations. A character network summarizes an agent across past episodes, a mental-state network represents the current episode, and a prediction network forecasts behavior and environment-relevant outcomes, including false-belief-sensitive behavior in simple worlds.
records.boundary_note: ToMnet is a functional predictive architecture for modeling other agents. Passing a gridworld analogue of a false-belief task does not establish phenomenal consciousness, genuine belief possession, human-equivalent social understanding, or a transparent symbolic representation of mental states.
records.claim_scope: Few-shot prediction and latent characterization of artificial agents from observed trajectories in simplified multi-agent environments.
records.evidence_profile: Held-out agent prediction, gridworld trajectories, consumption and action forecasts, meta-learning generalization, latent-character probes, and synthetic false-belief tasks.
open_questions: Do learned representations support systematic generalization beyond training populations and environment structure?
How should machine-ToM be evaluated without relying on superficial task cues?
Can the architecture represent communication, norms, emotion, recursive beliefs, and real human behavioral variability?

records.name: Feature Integration Theory of Attention
records.status: foundational historical theory · revised and actively tested
records.status_note: Feature Integration Theory established a major research program on binding and visual search. Strong serial-versus-parallel formulations do not exhaust current findings, and later versions introduced richer spatial selection and object-file mechanisms.
records.summary: Basic visual features are initially registered in parallel in separate feature maps. Focused spatial attention selects a location and binds co-located features into an object representation, explaining conjunction-search costs and illusory conjunctions when attention is limited.
records.boundary_note: This is an adjacent theory of visual attention and feature binding, not a general theory of consciousness. Its relevance is limited to mechanisms that organize perceptual content and to claims about when focal attention is required for binding.
records.claim_scope: Visual feature registration, spatial selection, feature binding, object formation, visual search, and illusory conjunctions.
records.evidence_profile: Feature and conjunction search, reaction-time set-size functions, divided-attention manipulations, illusory conjunctions, spatial cueing, and object-file experiments.
open_questions: Which bindings require focal spatial attention and which can arise through other grouping mechanisms?
How should the theory accommodate efficient conjunction search and scene structure?
What is the relationship between feature binding, reportability, and conscious perceptual organization?
